inBreve: {{Presente}} — the present tense: what is happening now or happens regularly: {{Lavoro a Lugano.}}
Form = **verb stem + person ending**.
Three verb groups — in {{-are}}, {{-ere}}, {{-ire}}, each with its own endings.

steps: Drop the infinitive ending: {{parlare → parl-}}, {{prendere → prend-}}, {{dormire → dorm-}}.
Add the ending for the person — see the table.
The subject pronoun is usually left out: the ending already shows the person. {{Parlo italiano.}} — I speak Italian.

tables.title: -ire verbs with -isc-
tables.note: -isc- appears only in io, tu, lui/lei and loro. Same pattern: {{capire}}, {{pulire}}, {{costruire}}, {{preferire}}.

uses.tr: I'm eating now.
Every day I take the bus.
Water boils at 100 degrees.
Tomorrow I'm leaving for Rome.
I've lived here for five years.

exceptions.title: Verbs in -care and -gare
exceptions.text: Before an ending starting with {{-i}}, add {{h}} to keep the hard sound [k], [g].

examples.tr: to look for → you look for, we look for
to pay → you pay, we pay

exceptions.title: Verbs in -iare
exceptions.text: Write only **one** {{i}}.

examples.tr: to eat → you eat, we eat
to study → you study

exceptions.title: Verbs in -cere and -gere
exceptions.text: Spelled regularly, but **the sound changes**: hard before {{-o}}, soft before {{-i}}, {{-e}}.

examples.tr: I read [g] — you read [dʒ]
I win [k] — you win [tʃ]

exceptions.title: Stress in loro
exceptions.text: The stress stays on the stem, not on the ending.

examples.tr: not «parlàno»

mistakes.why: Verbs in -iare keep only one i.
No «to be» here: lavoro already means «I work».

examples.tr: I work from 9 to 5.
Are you taking the train or the bus?
My wife reads a lot.
We sleep eight hours.
Do you understand Italian?
The children are watching TV.

inBreve: A reflexive verb is an action done **to yourself**: {{mi lavo}} = «I wash myself».
In the dictionary these verbs end in {{-si}}: {{alzarsi}}, {{vestirsi}}, {{divertirsi}}.
A pronoun always comes before the verb: {{mi, ti, si, ci, vi, si}}.

steps: Remove {{-si}} from the infinitive: {{alzarsi → alzare}}.
Conjugate the verb as usual: {{alzo, alzi, alza…}}
Put the matching pronoun in front: {{mi alzo}}, {{ti alzi}}, {{si alza}}.

tables.title: Presente: pronoun + verb
tables.note: The endings are the same as for normal -are, -ere, -ire verbs.

tables.title: Passato prossimo: always essere
tables.note: The participle agrees with the subject: {{-o / -a / -i / -e}}.

tables.title: With modal verbs — two options
tables.note: The pronoun goes before the modal verb or is attached to the end of the infinitive — both are correct.

uses.tr: I wash and get dressed.

uses.it: La mattina mi sveglio alle sette.
uses.tr: In the morning I wake up at seven.
I get angry when I'm tired.
We've known each other for ten years.

uses.it: Come ti chiami? — Mi chiamo Anna.
uses.tr: What's your name? — My name is Anna.

exceptions.title: Negation
exceptions.text: {{non}} goes **before** the pronoun.

examples.it: Non mi alzo presto la domenica.
examples.tr: I don't get up early on Sundays.

exceptions.title: With dovere, potere, volere
exceptions.text: Two correct options: the pronoun before the modal verb, or at the end of the infinitive ({{-si}} → {{-mi, -ti, -ci, -vi}}).

examples.it: Mi devo alzare presto. = Devo alzarmi presto.
examples.tr: I have to get up early.
Do you want to rest?

exceptions.title: Body parts and clothes
exceptions.text: Use the article, not «my».

examples.tr: I wash my hands.
He puts on his jacket.

exceptions.title: In the past tense
exceptions.text: Reflexive verbs in passato prossimo **always take essere**, and the participle agrees.

examples.tr: Anna got up late.
We had a lot of fun.

exceptions.title: One verb — two meanings
exceptions.text: Without {{-si}} the action is done to someone else; with {{-si}}, to yourself.

examples.tr: I wash the car. / I wash myself.
I call Marco. / My name is Marco.

mistakes.why: Without the pronoun it means «I lift (something)».
Reflexives in the past take only essere.
Body parts take the article, not «my».
The pronoun goes before devo or at the end of the infinitive.

examples.it: Mi sveglio alle 7, ma mi alzo alle 7:30.
examples.tr: I wake up at 7, but I get up at 7:30.
Do you like it in Lugano?

examples.it: Mio figlio si veste da solo.
examples.tr: My son gets dressed by himself.
We have a lot of fun at the seaside.
You worry too much!

examples.it: I bambini si addormentano alle nove.
examples.tr: The children fall asleep at nine.

g5-riflessivi-presente.summary: Pronoun + verb: **mi alzo, ti vesti, si diverte**. Negation: **non mi alzo**. Past: **mi sono alzato**.

inBreve: {{Passato prossimo}} is the past tense for **completed actions**: {{Ieri ho lavorato}} — “Yesterday I worked.”
It has two parts: {{avere}} or {{essere}} in the present + the **past participle** ({{participio}}).
With {{essere}} the participle agrees in gender and number: {{Anna è andata}}, {{i ragazzi sono andati}}.

steps: Choose the auxiliary: {{essere}} for movement, change of state and reflexive verbs; {{avere}} for everything else.
Put it in the present: {{ho, hai, ha…}} or {{sono, sei, è…}}
Form the participle: {{-are → -ato}}, {{-ere → -uto}}, {{-ire → -ito}}. Many common verbs are irregular (table below).
With {{essere}}, match the ending to the subject: {{-o, -a, -i, -e}}.

tables.title: How the participle is formed
tables.note: About 50 common verbs have an irregular participle — see “Participi irregolari”.

tables.title: Agreement with essere
tables.note: With {{avere}} the participle **does not change**: {{Anna ha mangiato}}.

uses.text: A completed action in the past
uses.it: Ieri ho lavorato fino alle sei.
uses.tr: Yesterday I worked until six.

uses.text: With time words: ieri, la settimana scorsa, due anni fa
uses.it: Due anni fa sono venuto in Svizzera.
uses.tr: Two years ago I came to Switzerland.

uses.it: Sono tornato a casa, ho cenato e sono uscito.
uses.tr: I came home, had dinner and went out.
Have you ever been to Rome?

uses.it: Stamattina ho bevuto solo un caffè.
uses.tr: This morning I only had a coffee.

exceptions.title: Reflexive verbs
exceptions.text: Always with {{essere}}.

examples.tr: I got up at seven.

exceptions.title: piacere and mancare
exceptions.text: Always with {{essere}}; the participle agrees with the thing liked.

examples.tr: I liked the pizza.
I liked the films.

exceptions.title: Mixed groups
exceptions.text: If there is at least one man in the group, the ending is {{-i}}.

examples.tr: Marco and Anna have arrived.

exceptions.title: cominciare and finire
exceptions.text: With an object — {{avere}}; when something starts by itself — {{essere}}.

examples.tr: I started the course.
The film has started.

exceptions.title: salire and scendere
exceptions.text: Getting on / off transport — {{essere}}; up or down the stairs — {{avere}}.

examples.tr: I got off the bus.
I went up the stairs.

exceptions.title: essere and stare
exceptions.text: They share one participle — {{stato}}.

examples.tr: I have been to Milan.
I was ill.

mistakes.why: andare is a verb of movement, so it takes essere.
With essere the participle agrees: Anna is feminine.
With avere the participle doesn't change.
piacere takes essere and the pronoun mi.

examples.it: Ieri sera abbiamo mangiato in un ristorante cinese.
examples.tr: Last night we ate at a Chinese restaurant.

examples.it: Mia sorella è nata a Kiev.
examples.tr: My sister was born in Kyiv.
Did you do your homework?

examples.it: Siamo rimasti a casa tutto il giorno.
examples.tr: We stayed at home all day.

examples.it: Ho preso il treno delle otto.
examples.tr: I took the eight o'clock train.
What happened?

g5-passato-prossimo-base.summary: **avere / essere + participle**. With essere it agrees: **è andato / è andata**. Irregular: **fatto, letto, preso, visto**.

verbs.tr: to go up; to get on
to go down; to get off

groups.title: Reflexives, piacere and mancare
groups.text: All reflexive verbs and piacere / mancare also take essere: {{mi sono alzato}}, {{mi è piaciuto}}.

groups.title: Everything else
groups.text: Verbs with an object ({{ho comprato il pane}}) and most verbs without one ({{ho dormito}}).

inBreve: The {{tu}} form means “you” (informal): use it with friends, colleagues and classmates.
For **every** verb in the present, the tu form ends in {{-i}}: {{parli, prendi, dormi}}.
With strangers and in formal places use {{Lei}} (polite “you”) with the 3rd person: {{Lei parla}}.

steps: Remove the infinitive ending: {{parlare → parl-}}.
Add {{-i}}: {{parli}}, {{prendi}}, {{dormi}}.
Reflexive verbs: {{ti}} + verb — {{ti alzi}}, {{ti svegli}}.

tables.title: One ending for all
tables.note: -isc- verbs keep it: {{pulire → pulisci}}, {{finire → finisci}}.

tables.title: Spelling: watch the letters
tables.note: {{-care / -gare}} add {{h}} to keep the hard sound; {{-iare}} keep only one {{i}}.

tables.title: Irregular: the tu form
tables.note: Full conjugations are in “I verbi irregolari”.

uses.tr: What time do you get up?
Where do you live?
Can you pass me the salt?
Are you coming to the cinema tonight?

exceptions.title: Tu or Lei
exceptions.text: With strangers, a doctor, at the bank — {{Lei}} + 3rd person. Written with a capital L.

examples.it: Come ti chiami? / Come si chiama?
examples.tr: What's your name? (informal / polite)
Where do you live? (informal / polite)

exceptions.title: No subject needed
exceptions.text: The {{-i}} ending already means “you”; say {{tu}} only for emphasis.

examples.tr: Do you speak Italian?
I work, and you?

exceptions.title: uscire
exceptions.text: The stem changes: {{esc-}} for io, tu, lui, loro; {{usc-}} for noi and voi.

examples.tr: Are you going out tonight? — Yes, we're going out together.

exceptions.title: -isc- verbs
exceptions.text: {{finire}}, {{pulire}}, {{preferire}}, {{capire}} have {{-isc-}} in the tu form.

examples.tr: Do you understand? — Yes, I do.

examples.it: Preferisci il tè o il caffè?
examples.tr: Do you prefer tea or coffee?

mistakes.why: The tu form always ends in -i.
-care: add h to keep the hard sound.
uscire: the tu stem is esc-.

examples.tr: How do you spend your day?

examples.it: A che ora finisci di lavorare?
examples.tr: What time do you finish work?
How do you get around town?
Are you paying or am I?
What do you do at the weekend?

examples.it: Vai a piedi o prendi l'autobus?
examples.tr: Do you walk or take the bus?

g5-presente-tu.summary: The tu form always ends in **-i**: **parli, prendi, dormi**. Watch **cerchi, paghi, mangi, pulisci**. Polite: **Lei + 3rd person**.

inBreve: The most common verbs are **irregular**: their forms have to be learned.
The {{noi}} and {{voi}} forms are usually almost regular: {{andiamo, andate}}.
A frequent pattern: {{-go}} in io and {{-gono}} in loro: {{vengo, vengono}}.

steps: Learn the {{io}} form — it shows the verb's type: {{faccio, vado, vengo}}.
The {{loro}} form looks like io: {{vado → vanno}}, {{vengo → vengono}}.
{{noi}} and {{voi}} almost always come from the infinitive: {{andare → andiamo}}, {{andate}}.

tables.title: fare, andare, stare
tables.note: {{dare}} works like {{stare}}: {{do}}, {{dai}}, {{dà}}, {{diamo}}, {{date}}, {{danno}}.

tables.title: With -g-: io -go, loro -gono
tables.note: Same type: {{tenere → tengo}}, {{scegliere → scelgo}}.

tables.title: uscire, bere, dire
tables.note: {{bere}} and {{dire}} use the old stems {{bev-}} and {{dic-}}.

uses.it: La mattina faccio colazione e vado al lavoro.
uses.tr: In the morning I have breakfast and go to work.

uses.text: andare a + infinitive — to go and do something
uses.tr: I'm going to bed.
How are you? — Fine, thanks.
It's cold today.

uses.text: venire — to come where the listener is
uses.tr: Are you coming to my place tonight?

exceptions.title: andare a / andare in
exceptions.text: Cities — {{a}}; countries and many places — {{in}}.

examples.it: Vado a Milano. / Vado in Italia.
examples.tr: I'm going to Milan. / I'm going to Italy.
I'm going to the bank, to the pharmacy.

exceptions.title: andare or venire
exceptions.text: {{venire}} is movement towards the listener or together with them.

examples.tr: I'm coming right away!
Are you coming with us?

exceptions.title: Expressions with fare
exceptions.text: {{fare}} often isn't translated as “do”.

examples.it: Faccio colazione e poi faccio la spesa.
examples.tr: I have breakfast and then do the shopping.
Shall we go for a walk?

exceptions.title: dà with an accent
exceptions.text: {{dà}} (gives) has an accent so it isn't confused with the preposition {{da}}.

examples.tr: He gives me his number.
What are you doing tonight?
We're going to the seaside on Sunday.
The children are staying at home.
I go out at eight.
I'm staying at home because it's raining.
What are you drinking? — A coffee.

g5-presente-irregular.summary: Learn the **io** form: **faccio, vado, sto, vengo, esco**. loro follows it: **vanno, vengono**. noi and voi are almost regular.

inBreve: {{potere}} — can, {{volere}} — want, {{dovere}} — must, have to.
They are followed by an **infinitive with no preposition**: {{posso venire}}, {{voglio dormire}}, {{devo lavorare}}.
All three are irregular in the present.

steps: Choose by meaning: can — {{potere}}, want — {{volere}}, have to — {{dovere}}.
Conjugate it (table below).
Add the second verb in the infinitive: {{devo partire}}.

tables.title: potere, volere, dovere
tables.note: {{può}} has an accent.

tables.title: sapere — to know how, to know
tables.note: {{sapere}} + infinitive = “know how to”: {{so nuotare}}.

uses.tr: May I come in?
I want to learn Italian.
I have to work tomorrow.
He wants a new car.
Can you close the window?

exceptions.title: vorrei — polite
exceptions.text: In shops, bars and restaurants say {{vorrei}} (“I would like”) instead of {{voglio}}. Learn it as a set phrase.

examples.tr: I'd like a coffee, please.

exceptions.title: potere or sapere
exceptions.text: {{potere}} — you are able to right now; {{sapere}} — you know how to.

examples.it: Oggi non posso nuotare, ho il raffreddore.
examples.tr: I can't swim today, I have a cold.
I can't swim (I don't know how).

exceptions.title: Negative
exceptions.text: {{non}} goes before the modal verb.

examples.tr: I can't come.

exceptions.title: With reflexive verbs
exceptions.text: The pronoun goes before the modal or on the end of the infinitive.

examples.tr: I have to get up.

mistakes.why: If you never learned how — sapere. Non posso means you can't right now.

examples.tr: Can you help me?
We want to go to the seaside.

examples.it: I bambini devono andare a letto presto.
examples.tr: The children have to go to bed early.
I can't come, I have to work.
Can you speak German?
I'd like to book a table.

g5-modali-presente.summary: **potere / volere / dovere + infinitive**, no preposition. Polite: **vorrei**. Know how to: **sapere**.

inBreve: {{Mi piace}} = “I like” (literally “it pleases me”). The subject is **what** is liked, not the person.
One thing or an infinitive — {{piace}}; several things — {{piacciono}}.
{{mancare}} works the same way: {{mi manca mio figlio}} — “I miss my son” (literally “my son is missing to me”).

steps: Find **who** likes it: {{mi}}, {{ti}}, {{gli}}, {{le}}, {{ci}}, {{vi}}, {{gli}}.
Find **what** is liked: one thing or several?
One thing or a verb — {{piace / manca}}; several — {{piacciono / mancano}}.

tables.title: piacere: to whom + what
tables.note: {{mancare}} works the same: {{mi manca / mi mancano}}.

tables.title: In the past
tables.note: In the passato prossimo use {{essere}}; the participle agrees with what was liked.

uses.tr: I like pizza.
We like travelling.
Do you like Italian films?
I miss my parents.
It needs salt.

exceptions.title: a me instead of mi
exceptions.text: For emphasis or contrast use {{a me, a te…}} instead of {{mi, ti}}.

examples.it: A me piace il mare, a lui la montagna.
examples.tr: I like the sea, he likes the mountains.

exceptions.title: Anche a me / Neanche a me
exceptions.text: To agree, don't say {{anch'io}} — say {{anche a me}} / {{neanche a me}}.

examples.it: Mi piace il caffè. — Anche a me!
examples.tr: I like coffee. — Me too!

examples.it: Non mi piace il freddo. — Neanche a me.
examples.tr: I don't like the cold. — Me neither.

exceptions.title: mancare with all persons
exceptions.text: The person who is missed is the subject.

examples.tr: I miss you.
Do you miss me?

exceptions.title: la famiglia, la gente
exceptions.text: Grammatically singular.

examples.tr: I miss my family.
I like the people here.

exceptions.title: mancare ≠ annoiarsi
exceptions.text: “To miss someone” — {{mancare}}; “to be bored” — {{annoiarsi}}.

examples.tr: I miss Kyiv. / I'm bored.

mistakes.why: The subject is pizza, not io.

mistakes.right: Mi piace il caffè. — Anche a me!
mistakes.why: Agreeing with piacere: anche a me.
The person missed is the subject.

examples.tr: Do you like your job?
She likes flowers.
We don't like getting up early.
Do you miss your city?

examples.it: Mi è piaciuta molto la festa.
examples.tr: I really enjoyed the party.

examples.it: Da bambino mi piacevano i cartoni animati.
examples.tr: As a child I liked cartoons.

g5-piacere-mancare.summary: **Mi piace** + one thing / infinitive, **mi piacciono** + several. mancare is the same: **mi manca / mi mancano**. Agreeing: **anche a me**.

inBreve: The definite article (“the”) goes before a noun when it's clear what we mean: {{il libro}} — “the book”.
The form depends on **gender**, **number** and the **first letter** of the word: {{il}}, {{lo}}, {{l'}}, {{la}}, {{i}}, {{gli}}, {{le}}.
Italian uses it more than English: {{mi piace la pizza}} (I like pizza), {{mi lavo le mani}} (I wash my hands).

steps: Find the gender: {{-o}} is usually masculine, {{-a}} usually feminine, {{-e}} — check the dictionary.
Look at the first letter: consonant, vowel, or {{z}}, {{s}} + consonant, {{gn}}, {{ps}}.
Pick the article from the table; in the plural — {{i}}, {{gli}} or {{le}}.

tables.title: Masculine
tables.note: Masculine plural has two articles: {{i}} and {{gli}}.

tables.title: Feminine
tables.note: Feminine plural is always {{le}}, never with an apostrophe: {{le amiche}}.

tables.title: How the noun changes
tables.note: Nouns in {{-e}} take {{-i}} in the plural, whatever the gender.

uses.tr: Take the book on the table.
I like music.
On Saturdays I go to the seaside.
I wash my hands.

uses.it: L'italiano è bello. La Svizzera è piccola.
uses.tr: Italian is beautiful. Switzerland is small.

exceptions.title: Relatives with “my, your”
exceptions.text: In the singular — **no** article: {{mia madre}}, {{tuo fratello}}; in the plural — with it: {{i miei fratelli}}.

examples.tr: My sister lives in Rome.

examples.it: I miei genitori sono in Ucraina.
examples.tr: My parents are in Ukraine.

exceptions.title: Nouns in -e
exceptions.text: You can't see the gender — learn the word with its article: {{il ristorante}}, {{la chiave}}, {{l'esame}} (m.), {{la notte}}.

examples.tr: newspaper · lesson

exceptions.title: Invariable nouns
exceptions.text: Foreign and shortened nouns don't change in the plural — only the article does: {{il film → i film}}, {{la foto → le foto}}, {{il bar → i bar}}.

examples.tr: I watch Italian films.

exceptions.title: Masculine nouns in -a
exceptions.text: {{il problema → i problemi}}, {{il programma}}, {{il pianeta}}.

examples.tr: The planet is in danger.

exceptions.title: la persona, la gente
exceptions.text: {{la persona}} is always feminine, even for a man; {{la gente}} is singular.

examples.tr: Marco is a nice person.

mistakes.why: Before a vowel, masculine plural takes gli.

examples.it: Prende gli ordini e parla con i clienti.
examples.tr: He takes the orders and talks to the customers.

examples.it: Porta il cibo e le bevande.
examples.tr: She brings the food and the drinks.
The backpack is on the chair.
The students are taking the exam.
Anna's friend is a doctor.
Lessons finish at six.

g1-articoli-determinativi.summary: Masculine: **il / lo / l'** → **i / gli / gli**. Feminine: **la / l'** → **le**. Before a vowel — **l'**, before z and s + consonant — **lo**.

inBreve: The prepositions {{a, di, da, in, su}} **merge** with the definite article: {{a + il = al}}.
The article keeps its shape: {{lo → allo}}, {{l' → all'}}, {{gli → agli}}, {{le → alle}}.
{{in}} becomes {{ne-}}: {{nel, nella}}; {{di}} becomes {{de-}}: {{del, della}}.

steps: Choose the preposition by meaning (see “Meanings”).
Find the noun's article: {{il}}, {{lo}}, {{l'}}, {{la}}, {{i}}, {{gli}}, {{le}}.
Combine them using the table: {{su + la = sulla}}, {{in + gli = negli}}.

tables.title: Singular
tables.note: Before a vowel — with an apostrophe: {{all'una}}, {{dell'amico}}, {{nell'ufficio}}.

tables.title: Plural
tables.note: {{con}} and {{per}} don't merge: {{con gli amici}}, {{per il pranzo}}.

tables.title: Meanings

items.tr: in the bag · in the park

tables.note: {{a}} — when, where to; {{di}} — whose; {{da}} — to someone's place, since; {{in}} — in, inside; {{su}} — on.

uses.tr: I work from nine to five.
I'm going to the supermarket.

uses.it: La macchina del mio vicino è rossa.
uses.tr: My neighbour's car is red.
Tomorrow I'm going to the dentist's.
The keys are on the table.

exceptions.title: No article, no merging
exceptions.text: Set phrases: {{a casa}}, {{a letto}}, {{a scuola}}, {{in banca}}, {{in ufficio}}, {{in città}}, {{in centro}}.

examples.it: Vado a casa. / Vado in banca.
examples.tr: I'm going home. / I'm going to the bank.

exceptions.title: Clock times
exceptions.text: Clock times always take the article: {{alle otto}}, {{dalle nove}}; but {{a mezzogiorno}}, {{a mezzanotte}}.

examples.it: Pranzo a mezzogiorno e ceno alle otto.
examples.tr: I have lunch at noon and dinner at eight.

exceptions.title: Cities and countries
exceptions.text: City — {{a}}, country — {{in}}, no article.

examples.tr: I live in Lugano, in Switzerland.

exceptions.title: da + person
exceptions.text: “To / at someone's place” — {{da}}, with the article before a job title.

examples.tr: Tonight we're having dinner at Marco's.
I'm going to the doctor's.

mistakes.why: in banca is a set phrase, no article.

examples.tr: He goes to the workshop at eight.
He works until one p.m.

examples.it: Va a letto prima delle undici.
examples.tr: He goes to bed before eleven.
The cat sleeps on the sofa.

examples.it: Nel fine settimana andiamo dai nonni.
examples.tr: At the weekend we go to our grandparents'.

examples.it: Il treno parte dal binario tre.
examples.tr: The train leaves from platform three.

g4-preposizioni-articolate.summary: **a, di, da, in, su + article = one word**: al, del, dal, nel, sul. Times always **alle**. **a casa, in banca** — no article.

inBreve: Some verbs link to a second verb with a preposition: {{comincio a lavorare}}, {{finisco di lavorare}}.
**Learn the preposition together with the verb** — there's no general rule.
After {{volere}}, {{potere}}, {{dovere}}, {{sapere}}, {{piacere}} — **no preposition**: {{voglio dormire}}.

steps: Conjugate the first verb: {{comincio, cominci…}}
Add that verb's preposition: {{a}} or {{di}}.
The second verb is always an infinitive: {{a lavorare}}, {{di studiare}}.

tables.title: Verb + a
tables.note: Movement + purpose also takes {{a}}: {{vado a mangiare}}, {{vengo a trovarti}}.

tables.title: Verb + di
tables.note: {{smettere di}} — to stop / quit: {{smetto di fumare}}.

tables.title: No preposition
tables.note: Modal verbs and {{piacere}} take the infinitive directly.

uses.it: Domani comincio a lavorare alle sette.
uses.tr: Tomorrow I start work at seven.
I finish work late.
I decided to learn Italian.
Shall we go and have a pizza?

exceptions.title: pensare a / pensare di
exceptions.text: {{pensare a}} + someone — to think about; {{pensare di}} + infinitive — to plan to.

examples.tr: I'm thinking about my mother.
I'm thinking of leaving tomorrow.

exceptions.title: In the past
exceptions.text: The preposition stays: {{ho cominciato a lavorare}}, {{ho finito di studiare}}.

examples.tr: It started to rain.

exceptions.title: riuscire a
exceptions.text: “To manage to”. Conjugated like {{uscire}}: {{riesco, riesci, riesce}}.

examples.tr: I can't get to sleep.

exceptions.title: Negative
exceptions.text: {{non}} before the infinitive changes the meaning: “try not to…”.

inBreve: Short adverbs go **between** the auxiliary and the participle: {{ho già mangiato}}.

inBreve: The {{imperfetto}} is the past tense for **describing**: what things were like, what you used to do, what was going on.
Easy to form: infinitive stem + {{-vo}}, {{-vi}}, {{-va}}, {{-vamo}}, {{-vate}}, {{-vano}}.
Almost all verbs are regular. The special ones: {{essere}} ({{ero}}), {{fare}} ({{facevo}}), {{bere}}, {{dire}}.

steps: Drop {{-re}}: {{ascoltare → ascolta-}}, {{volere → vole-}}, {{sentire → senti-}}.
Add the ending: {{-vo}}, {{-vi}}, {{-va}}, {{-vamo}}, {{-vate}}, {{-vano}}.
Reflexives keep the pronoun: {{mi alzavo}}, {{si vestiva}}.

tables.note: Same endings for {{-are}}, {{-ere}}, {{-ire}}.

g5-imperfetto.summary: Stem + **-vo, -vi, -va, -vamo, -vate, -vano**. Special: **ero, facevo, bevevo, dicevo**. For descriptions, habits and background.

inBreve: {{Passato prossimo}} — **what happened**: an event, once, finished, it moves the story on.
{{Imperfetto}} — **what it was like**: setting, habit, state, background.
Often together: {{mentre leggevo}} (background), {{è arrivato un messaggio}} (event).

steps: Ask “what happened?” — {{passato prossimo}}.
Ask “what was it like? what did I use to do?” — {{imperfetto}}.

inBreve: {{quindi}}, {{perciò}}, {{allora}}, {{dunque}} all mean “so, therefore”.
They go **between the cause and the result**: {{pioveva}}, {{quindi}} {{sono rimasto a casa}}.
In the past: the cause (a state) — {{imperfetto}}, the result — {{passato prossimo}}.

steps: Say the cause: {{ero stanco}}.
Add a comma and the connector: {{, quindi}}.
Say the result: {{sono andato a letto}}.

inBreve: To describe a person you need three verbs: {{essere}} (what they're like), {{avere}} (what they have), {{portare}} (what they wear).

Glasses, beard, earrings — {{portare}}: {{porta gli occhiali}}.

g2-descrizione-persona.summary: **è** alto, gentile · **ha** 22 anni, gli occhi verdi · **porta** gli occhiali · **fa** il meccanico. Adjective after the noun, and it agrees.

inBreve: {{Prima}} (before) — {{imperfetto}}: how it was.
{{Ora}}, {{adesso}} (now) — {{presente}}: how it is.
The change itself — {{passato prossimo}}: {{è ingrassato}}, {{ha cambiato stile}}.

steps: Describe the past: {{prima aveva}} {{i capelli neri}}.
Describe the present: {{ora ha i capelli rossi}}.
Say what happened: {{ha colorato i capelli}}.

tables.title: Prima — ora

items.tr: had no beard → now has one
was happy → now a bit sad

tables.note: Left — {{imperfetto}}, right — {{presente}}.

tables.title: Verbs of change — essere
tables.note: All take {{essere}}; the participle agrees: {{mia madre è invecchiata}}.

tables.title: Comparing
tables.note: {{-issimo}} = “very”: {{lungo → lunghissimo}} ({{-go}}, {{-co}} + {{h}}).

uses.tr: I used to live in Ukraine.
Now I live in Switzerland.
I've changed a lot.

uses.it: Ora è più tranquillo di prima.
uses.tr: Now he's calmer than before.

exceptions.title: cambiare: avere or essere
exceptions.text: Changed something — {{avere}}; changed yourself — {{essere}}.

examples.it: Ha cambiato stile. / È cambiato molto.
examples.tr: He changed his style. / He's changed a lot.

exceptions.title: crescere: what grew
exceptions.text: The subject is what grew: {{gli è cresciuta la barba}}.

examples.tr: He's grown a beard.

exceptions.title: ancora and non più
exceptions.text: {{ancora}} — still; {{non… più}} — no longer.

examples.tr: He still wears glasses.
He doesn't wear glasses any more.

exceptions.title: il sopracciglio → le sopracciglia
exceptions.text: The plural is feminine in {{-a}}.

examples.tr: She has dark eyebrows.

mistakes.wrong: Prima ha avuto i capelli neri.

examples.it: Prima ero basso, poi sono cresciuto e sono diventato alto.
examples.tr: I used to be short, then I grew and became tall.

examples.it: Prima aveva i capelli lunghi, adesso li ha corti.
examples.tr: She used to have long hair, now it's short.
My father has lost a lot of weight.

examples.it: Prima si vestiva in modo casual, ora è elegante.
examples.tr: He used to dress casually, now he's smart.

examples.it: Mia nonna è invecchiata, ma è ancora bellissima.
examples.tr: My grandmother has aged, but she's still very beautiful.

examples.it: Non porto più le lenti a contatto.
examples.tr: I don't wear contact lenses any more.

g5-prima-ora.summary: **Prima** + imperfetto, **ora** + present, the change — **passato prossimo**. Verbs of change take **essere**: è ingrassato, è diventata.

inBreve: {{Futuro semplice}} is the future tense: {{domani partirò}} — “I'll leave tomorrow”.
One set of endings for all: {{-ò}}, {{-ai}}, {{-à}}, {{-emo}}, {{-ete}}, {{-anno}}.
In {{-are}} verbs the {{a}} becomes {{e}}: {{parlare → parlerò}}.

steps: Drop the final {{-e}}: {{partire → partir-}}, {{prendere → prender-}}.
For {{-are}}, change {{a}} to {{e}}: {{arrivare → arriver-}}.
Add the ending: {{-ò}}, {{-ai}}, {{-à}}, {{-emo}}, {{-ete}}, {{-anno}}.

tables.title: Regular verbs
tables.note: The accent in {{io}} and {{lui}} is written: {{arriverò}}, {{arriverà}}.

tables.title: Special stems
tables.note: Same endings — only the stem changes.

tables.title: Spelling
tables.note: {{-care}}, {{-gare}} add {{h}}; {{-ciare}}, {{-giare}} drop the {{i}}.

uses.tr: My friends will arrive tomorrow.

uses.it: L'anno prossimo mi iscriverò a un corso di tedesco.
uses.tr: Next year I'll sign up for a German course.
I'll help you!
It will rain tomorrow.

uses.it: Dove sarà Marta? — Sarà al lavoro.
uses.tr: Where can Marta be? — She's probably at work.

exceptions.title: Present instead of future
exceptions.text: For the near future, Italians often use the {{presente}}.

examples.tr: I'm going to the seaside tomorrow.

exceptions.title: Guessing
exceptions.text: The {{futuro}} can mean “probably now”: {{saranno le otto}}.

examples.it: Che ore sono? — Saranno le otto.
examples.tr: What time is it? — It must be about eight.

exceptions.title: Signal words
exceptions.text: {{domani}}, {{la settimana prossima}}, {{l'anno prossimo}}, {{tra due anni}}, {{in futuro}}.

examples.it: Tra due anni parlerò bene l'italiano.
examples.tr: In two years I'll speak Italian well.

exceptions.title: da grande
exceptions.text: “When I grow up” — for children's dreams.

examples.tr: When I grow up I'll be a doctor.
Tomorrow I'll start a new job.

examples.it: Metteremo da parte un po' di soldi.
examples.tr: We'll put some money aside.

examples.it: Il treno partirà dal binario dieci.
examples.tr: The train will leave from platform ten.
This summer we'll go to Sicily.
You must be tired after the journey.
You'll see, everything will be fine!

g5-futuro-semplice.summary: Stem + **-ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno**. In -are **a → e**. Special: **sarò, farò, andrò, avrò, verrò, vorrò**.

inBreve: Weather verbs have **no subject**: {{piove}} means “it's raining”.
Always **3rd person singular**: {{piove}}, {{pioverà}}, {{pioveva}}.
**Yesterday** takes the {{imperfetto}}: weather is background — {{ieri pioveva}}.

steps: Pick the expression: {{piovere}}, {{fare caldo}}, {{c'è il sole}}.
Look at the time word: {{oggi}}, {{domani}}, {{ieri}}.
Use the “lui” form: {{piove}} · {{pioverà}} · {{pioveva}}.

tables.title: Oggi · domani · ieri
tables.note: {{nevicare → nevicherà}}: add {{h}}, like {{cercherò}}.

tables.title: Che tempo fa?
tables.note: Three ways: a verb ({{piove}}), {{fare}} + word ({{fa caldo}}), {{c'è}} + noun ({{c'è vento}}).

tables.title: Weather or person?
tables.note: Weather — {{fare}}; a person — {{avere}}.

uses.tr: What's the weather like today?
Tomorrow it will rain in the north.
Yesterday it was cold and snowing.

uses.it: Pioveva, quindi sono rimasto a casa.
uses.tr: It was raining, so I stayed home.
When I was a child it always snowed in winter.

exceptions.title: Passato prossimo
exceptions.text: A finished event: {{è piovuto}} or {{ha piovuto}} — both are correct.

examples.tr: It rained a lot last night.

exceptions.title: The sky
exceptions.text: The sky is described with {{essere}}: {{è nuvoloso}}, {{è sereno}}.

examples.tr: The sky is clear today.

exceptions.title: Present for tomorrow
exceptions.text: In speech {{domani piove}} is fine too; {{pioverà}} sounds like a forecast.

examples.tr: It's raining tomorrow, let's stay home.

examples.it: Oggi piove, ma domani ci sarà il sole.
examples.tr: It's raining today, but tomorrow it'll be sunny.

examples.it: Ieri nevicava e faceva molto freddo.
examples.tr: Yesterday it was snowing and very cold.

examples.it: In estate in Ticino fa caldo.
examples.tr: In summer it's hot in Ticino.
What will the weather be like on Saturday?
It's windy: close the window!

examples.it: Faceva bel tempo, quindi siamo andati al lago.
examples.tr: The weather was nice, so we went to the lake.

g5-meteo.summary: **Oggi** piove · **domani** pioverà · **ieri** pioveva. Weather: a verb, **fare** + word, or **c'è** + noun.

inBreve: {{Esserci}} = {{essere}} + {{ci}}: “**there is / there are**”.
The form depends on **what there is**: one — {{c'è}}, several — {{ci sono}}.
Three tenses: {{c'è}} → {{c'era}} → {{ci sarà}}.

steps: Find **what** there is: {{un bar}} (one) or {{due bar}} (several).
Choose the tense: {{oggi}}, {{ieri}}, {{domani}}.
Take the form from the table: {{c'era}} / {{c'erano}}…

tables.title: Tre tempi
tables.note: Before {{e}} — {{c'}}: {{c'è}}, {{c'era}}. Before {{s}} — {{ci}}: {{ci sono}}, {{ci sarà}}.

tables.title: Esempi

items.tr: There were lots of people at the party.
There will be a party tomorrow.
The children will be there too.

tables.note: Look at the word **after** it: {{un bar}} → {{c'è}}, {{molti turisti}} → {{ci sono}}.

tables.title: È, c'è or sta?

items.tr: è describes: the bar is closed
c'è — does it exist: is there a bar?

tables.note: {{malato}} changes: {{malata}}, {{malati}}. {{male}} never does.

tables.title: Yesterday: imperfetto

items.tr: She was ill yesterday ↔ She felt unwell yesterday

tables.note: A past state — {{imperfetto}}: {{era}}, {{stava}}.

uses.it: Nel mio quartiere c'è una farmacia.
uses.tr: There's a pharmacy in my neighbourhood.
Excuse me, is there a toilet?
Is Marco there? — No, he isn't.
There used to be a cinema here.
There will be a party on Saturday.

exceptions.title: Negation
exceptions.text: {{non}} goes before {{ci}}: {{non c'è}}, {{non ci sono}}.

examples.tr: There's no milk in the fridge.

exceptions.title: Passato prossimo
exceptions.text: An event: {{c'è stato}}, {{ci sono stati}}.

examples.tr: There was an accident yesterday.

exceptions.title: Ci sei?
exceptions.text: About a person: “will you be there / are you there?” — {{ci sei?}}

examples.it: Ci sei stasera? — Sì, ci sono.
examples.tr: Will you be there tonight? — Yes, I will.

examples.it: In classe ci sono quindici studenti.
examples.tr: There are fifteen students in the class.

examples.it: Scusi, c'è una farmacia qui vicino?
examples.tr: Excuse me, is there a pharmacy nearby?

examples.it: Quando ero piccolo, qui c'era un parco.
examples.tr: When I was little, there was a park here.

examples.it: Alla riunione ci saranno anche i direttori.
examples.tr: The directors will be at the meeting too.
No problem!
I'm not coming today: I feel unwell.

g5-esserci.summary: **c'è / ci sono** → **c'era / c'erano** → **ci sarà / ci saranno**. One — c'è, several — ci sono. **È** describes, **c'è** means “there is”.
